Patrick Flynn's birthplace is disputed — the 1850 and 1860 censuses both record Ireland, while his 1908 death certificate records Pennsylvania. Resolving this matters for understanding Patrick's origins and his family's immigration history, which bears directly on identifying his parents.

The 1850 census (a_002), completed when Patrick was about 5, records his birthplace as Ireland; the household informant — almost certainly Thomas Flynn or his wife — told the enumerator this directly. The 1860 census (a_009), taken when Patrick was about 15, repeats the same birthplace through the same household. The 1908 death certificate (a_012) states Pennsylvania; the named informant is James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law, who signed the certificate.

The census household informants had the strongest epistemic standing for this fact: they either witnessed Patrick's birth in Ireland or emigrated with him as an infant, and they reported 'Ireland' consistently across two independent census years. Brown was reporting in 1908 a birth that occurred 63 years earlier, which he did not witness and could not have known firsthand. His report is uncorroborated — no other source supports Pennsylvania. Both the 'uncorroborated single item' and 'substantially less credible informant' rationales apply to set aside a_012.

The Pennsylvania answer reflects the well-documented pattern of immigration origin confusion. Brown knew Patrick exclusively as a Pennsylvania resident throughout his adult life. Without access to the family's pre-immigration history, he associated Patrick with Pennsylvania — the only home he had known. A son-in-law reporting a birth he did not witness, 63 years after the event, where the family's American home was the only locally familiar answer, is precisely the informant type whose foreign-birth claims carry the least weight.
